rule_en: Use the verb be to say who people are, where they are from and how they feel. Subject pronouns (I, you, he, she, it, we, they) always come before the verb. In everyday English we usually use contractions: I'm, you're, he's.
structure: I + am / he, she, it + is / we, you, they + are
examples_en: I'm Karim and I'm from Tajikistan.
She's a new student in our class.
We're very happy today.
They're from Canada.
tip: Remember: every English sentence needs a subject — say 'It is cold', not 'Is cold'.

questions.text: Choose the correct form: I ___ twenty years old.
Choose the correct form: My sister ___ a nurse.
Choose the correct form: You and Ali ___ late.
Choose the correct contraction: 'They are here' = ___
Choose the correct pronoun: ___ is my brother.
questions.explanation: Subject pronoun 'he' comes before the verb.
English sentences need a subject: 'It is Monday'.

rule_en: Make be negative with not: I'm not, he isn't, they aren't. Make questions by putting be before the subject: Are you...? Is she...? Answer with short answers: Yes, I am. / No, she isn't.
structure: negative: subject + be + not; question: Be + subject...?
examples_en: I'm not from Russia — I'm from Uzbekistan.
He isn't at home now.
Are you tired? — No, I'm not.
Is this seat free? — Yes, it is.
tip: In short positive answers don't use contractions: say 'Yes, I am', not 'Yes, I'm'.

questions.text: Choose the negative: She ___ a teacher.
Choose the question: ___ they from Italy?
questions.explanation: 'They' takes 'are'; the verb goes first in questions.

questions.text: Choose the short answer: Are you hungry? — Yes, I ___.
questions.explanation: Short answer: Yes, I am (no contraction).

questions.text: Choose the negative: We ___ ready yet.
Choose the question: ___ your phone new?

questions.explanation: Short negative answer: No, she isn't.

rule_en: Possessive adjectives (my, your, his, her, its, our, their) show who something belongs to. They come before a noun and never change for plural: my book, my books.
examples_en: My email address is on this card.
What's your surname?
Her phone number is easy to remember.
Their teacher is from London.
tip: Don't confuse its (possessive) and it's (= it is).

questions.text: Choose the correct word: ___ name is Dilshod. (he)
Choose the correct word: We love ___ new flat.
Choose the correct word: The dog is in ___ house.
Choose the correct word: ___ books are on the table. (they)
Choose the correct word: She lives with ___ parents.

rule_en: Most nouns add -s in the plural: key → keys. Nouns ending in -s, -sh, -ch, -x add -es: watch → watches. Consonant + y changes to -ies: city → cities. Some plurals are irregular: man → men, woman → women, child → children, person → people.
examples_en: There are two windows in my room.
I need three boxes for these books.
The children are in the garden.
Most people here speak two languages.
tip: Learn irregular plurals by heart — they are very common words.

options: The keys are on the table.
The keyes are on the table.
The key are on the table.
questions.answer: The keys are on the table.

rule_en: Adjectives describe nouns. They go before the noun or after be, and they never change for plural: a black cat, black cats. Modifiers very, really and quite make an adjective stronger or weaker and go before it.
examples_en: It's a really interesting film.
These shoes are quite expensive.
My city is very old and beautiful.
He drives an expensive German car.
tip: Quite is weaker than very: quite good < very good < really good.

options: She has a very nice voice.
She has a nice very voice.
She has very a voice nice.
questions.answer: She has a very nice voice.

questions.text: Which is the weakest? 'The food is ___ good.'

questions.explanation: The modifier goes directly before the adjective.
Size usually comes before colour: small red car.

rule_en: Use the imperative (base verb) to give instructions and orders: Sit down. Open the window. The negative is Don't + verb: Don't worry. Use Let's + verb to make a suggestion for you and other people: Let's go home.
examples_en: Turn off your phone, please.
Don't be nervous — it's only a test.
Let's have a break.
Slow down! You walk too fast.
tip: Add 'please' to sound polite: 'Close the door, please.'

questions.explanation: Imperative = base verb without a subject.

questions.text: Choose the suggestion: ___ watch a film tonight.
questions.explanation: Let's + verb suggests doing something together.
With 'be' the negative imperative is 'Don't be'.
The negative of Let's is Let's not + verb.

options: To listen and to repeat you.
questions.explanation: Instructions use the base form of the verb.

rule_en: Use the present simple for habits, routines and facts. With I/you/we/they use the base verb; with he/she/it add -s. The negative is don't / doesn't + base verb.
examples_en: I cook dinner every evening.
My father works in a bank.
We don't watch TV in the morning.
She doesn't drink coffee.
tip: After doesn't the verb loses its -s: 'She doesn't work', not 'She doesn't works'.

questions.text: Choose the correct form: He ___ breakfast at seven.

questions.explanation: With 'I' the negative is don't + verb.

questions.text: Choose the negative: She ___ in this office.
Choose the correct form: My mother ___ English at school.

options: We don't go out on Mondays.
We doesn't go out on Mondays.
We don't goes out on Mondays.
questions.answer: We don't go out on Mondays.

rule_en: Make present simple questions with do / does + subject + base verb: Do you work? Does she work? Use do with I/you/we/they and does with he/she/it. The main verb never takes -s in questions.
examples_en: Do you like your job?
Does he travel a lot?
Where do they have lunch?
What time does the shop open?
tip: Answer with do/does, not the main verb: 'Yes, I do', not 'Yes, I like'.

questions.text: Choose the question: ___ you work at weekends?
Choose the question: ___ she speak German?
Choose the short answer: Do they study here? — Yes, they ___.

options: What time does the film start?
What time do the film start?
What time the film does start?
questions.answer: What time does the film start?

topic: word order in questions; question words
rule_en: English questions follow a fixed order: (Question word) + auxiliary + subject + verb. Common question words: What, Where, When, Who, Why, How, How much, How many, What kind of.
examples_en: Why do you get up so early?
How many brothers does she have?
What kind of music do they play?
When does the lesson finish?
tip: Remember ASI: Auxiliary before Subject In questions.

questions.text: Choose the question word: ___ do you visit your grandparents? — Once a month.
Choose the question word: ___ many students are in your class?

options: What kind of films does he like?
What kind of films he likes?
What kind of films do he likes?
questions.answer: What kind of films does he like?

rule_en: Add 's to a person to show possession: Anna's bag. For regular plurals add only an apostrophe: my parents' house. Ask about possession with Whose: Whose phone is this?
examples_en: This is my brother's room.
Whose keys are these? — They're Omar's.
My grandparents' photos are very old.
Karim's wife works in a hospital.
tip: 'Whose' asks about the owner; 'Who's' means 'Who is' — they sound the same!

questions.text: Choose the correct form: This is ___ car. (my father)
questions.explanation: Add 's to the owner: my father's car.

questions.text: Choose the question: ___ jacket is this?
Choose the correct form: my ___ house (parents, plural)
Choose the correct answer: Whose books are these? — They're ___.

options: My sisters' son is three years my.

topic: prepositions of time (at, in, on) and place (at, in, to)
rule_en: Time: at + clock time (at six), on + day or date (on Monday), in + month, season, year (in July). Place: in + city or country (in Dushanbe), at + a point or place (at work, at home), to + movement (go to school).
examples_en: I get up at half past six.
We have English on Tuesdays.
She was born in 1998.
He goes to the gym after work.
tip: Say 'at night' but 'in the morning / afternoon / evening'.

questions.text: Choose the preposition: The film starts ___ eight o'clock.
Choose the preposition: My birthday is ___ May.
Choose the preposition: We don't work ___ Sundays.
Choose the preposition: She lives ___ Samarkand.
Choose the preposition: The children go ___ school by bus.
Choose the preposition: My mother is ___ work now.
questions.explanation: at + place where someone is: at work.

topic: position of adverbs and expressions of frequency
rule_en: Adverbs of frequency (always, usually, often, sometimes, hardly ever, never) go before the main verb but after be. Longer expressions (every day, twice a week, once a month) usually go at the end of the sentence.
structure: subject + adverb + verb / be + adverb; expression at the end
examples_en: I usually have lunch at one.
She is never late for work.
They visit their grandmother every Sunday.
We go to the cinema twice a month.
tip: 'Never' and 'hardly ever' are already negative — don't add 'not'.

questions.explanation: Frequency adverb before the main verb.

options: They are usually at home in the evening.
They usually are at home in the evening.
Usually they are at usually home.
questions.answer: They are usually at home in the evening.

options: We go shopping once a week.
We once a week go shopping.
We go once shopping a week.
questions.answer: We go shopping once a week.
questions.explanation: Longer expressions go at the end.

options: I never drink coffee at night.
I don't never drink coffee at night.
I drink never coffee at night.
questions.answer: I never drink coffee at night.
questions.explanation: 'Never' goes before the verb and needs no 'not'.

questions.text: Which means about 90% of the time?

options: She is always happy on Fridays.
She always is happy on Fridays.
Always she is on Fridays happy.
questions.answer: She is always happy on Fridays.

rule_en: Use can + base verb to talk about ability (I can swim) and permission (You can park here). The negative is can't (cannot). Can is the same for all persons and never takes -s or 'to'.
examples_en: She can play the guitar really well.
I can't come to the meeting tomorrow.
You can buy a newspaper at the station.
Can we sit here? — Yes, of course.
tip: Stress: in positive sentences 'can' is weak /kən/; 'can't' is strong /kɑːnt/.

questions.text: Choose the correct form: My grandmother ___ use a smartphone.
questions.explanation: 'Can' is the same for all persons.

questions.text: Choose the negative: I ___ find my glasses.
questions.explanation: The negative of can is can't.

questions.text: Choose the short answer: Can they swim? — No, they ___.

options: You can pay by card here.
You can to pay by card here.
You can paying by card here.
questions.answer: You can pay by card here.

rule_en: Use the present continuous (be + verb-ing) for actions happening now or around now: I'm reading. She's making noise. Spelling: make → making, sit → sitting, study → studying.
examples_en: The neighbours are playing loud music.
I'm looking for my keys.
She's talking on the phone right now.
We're waiting for the bus.
tip: Use time markers now, right now, at the moment with the present continuous.

questions.text: Choose the correct form: He ___ a shower now.
Choose the correct form: They ___ football in the park.
Choose the negative: I ___ TV — I'm working.

options: The baby is crying at the moment.
The baby crying at the moment.
The baby is cry at the moment.
questions.answer: The baby is crying at the moment.

rule_en: Present simple = habits, routines, facts (I work every day). Present continuous = actions now or temporary situations (I'm working today from home). Some verbs (like, want, know, need) are not normally used in the continuous.
structure: habit → present simple; now/temporary → present continuous
examples_en: It usually rains a lot in spring.
Take an umbrella — it's raining.
She works in a school, but this week she's working from home.
I want a cup of tea.
tip: State verbs like 'want, like, know, need' stay in the present simple.

questions.text: Choose the correct form: Listen! Someone ___ the piano.
Choose the correct form: The shops ___ at 9 a.m. every day.
Choose the correct form: I ___ this song — turn it up!
questions.explanation: 'Like' is a state verb → present simple.

questions.text: Choose the correct form: This month she ___ in a hotel.
Choose the correct form: What ___ you ___ at the moment?

options: It snows a lot here in winter.
It is snowing a lot here in winter usually.
It snow a lot here in winter.
questions.answer: It snows a lot here in winter.

rule_en: Object pronouns (me, you, him, her, it, us, them) replace a noun after a verb or preposition: I know him. Listen to me. Don't use the subject pronoun in this position.
examples_en: I love this story — read it again!
She calls her mother and talks to her every day.
Our teacher gives us a lot of homework.
Do you know them? — Yes, they're my neighbours.
tip: Pairs to remember: I→me, he→him, she→her, we→us, they→them.

questions.text: Choose the correct pronoun: This is Amir. I work with ___.
Choose the correct pronoun: We're here! Can you see ___?
Choose the correct pronoun: I like these photos. Look at ___.
Choose the correct pronoun: She's my best friend. I tell ___ everything.

options: Please help me with this exercise.
Please help I with this exercise.
Please help my with this exercise.
questions.answer: Please help me with this exercise.

questions.text: Choose the correct pronoun: The film is great. Don't miss ___!

rule_en: After like, love, hate and enjoy we use verb + -ing: I like dancing. For dates use ordinal numbers: the first, the second, the third, the fourth... We write '5 May' but say 'the fifth of May'.
structure: like/love/hate/enjoy + verb-ing; the + ordinal + of + month
examples_en: I love getting presents.
He hates waiting in queues.
Her birthday is on the third of June.
New Year is on the first of January.
tip: Ordinals to remember: 1st first, 2nd second, 3rd third, 5th fifth, 12th twelfth, 20th twentieth.

questions.text: Choose the correct form: She enjoys ___ new people.
Choose the correct form: I hate ___ up early on Sundays.
How do we say the date '1 March'?

options: We love swimming in the sea.
We love swim in the sea.
We love to swimming in the sea.
questions.answer: We love swimming in the sea.

rule_en: Use be (am/is/are) with nouns, adjectives and -ing forms: She's a singer. Are you tired? Use do/does with other verbs in questions and negatives: Do you sing? He doesn't play. Don't mix them.
examples_en: Are you a musician? — Yes, I am.
Do you play in a band? — No, I don't.
She isn't listening to music now.
He doesn't like jazz.
tip: If the sentence has another main verb, use do/does; if not, use be.

questions.text: Choose the correct question: ___ you like rock music?
Choose the correct question: ___ you a student?
Choose the correct negative: He ___ speak French.
Choose the correct negative: They ___ at the concert.
questions.explanation: 'At the concert' has no verb → be.

questions.text: Choose the correct question: ___ she singing now?

I'm not play the piano, but I do a good listener.
I don't a pianist, but I am play well.
questions.answer: I don't play the piano, but I'm a good listener.

topic: past simple of be: was / were
rule_en: The past of am/is is was; the past of are is were. Negative: wasn't / weren't. Questions: Was she...? Were you...? Use it to talk about states and places in the past.
examples_en: I was at my cousin's wedding yesterday.
The photos were beautiful.
Where were you last night?
The museum wasn't open on Monday.
tip: 'There was' + singular, 'there were' + plural.

questions.text: Choose the correct form: She ___ a famous writer.
Choose the correct form: We ___ very tired after the trip.
Choose the negative: The tickets ___ expensive.
Choose the question: ___ you at school yesterday?
Choose the short answer: Was the concert good? — Yes, it ___.

options: There were a lot of people at the party.
There was a lot of people at the party.
There is a lot of people at the party yesterday.
questions.answer: There were a lot of people at the party.

rule_en: Regular verbs add -ed in the past simple: work → worked. Spelling: live → lived, study → studied, stop → stopped. The form is the same for all persons. Use past time expressions: yesterday, last week, two years ago.
examples_en: We visited my uncle last weekend.
She studied French at university.
The bus stopped in front of the hotel.
I called you an hour ago.
tip: 'ago' goes after the time period: two days ago, not ago two days.

options: I watched a film last night.
I watch a film last night.
I am watched a film last night.
questions.answer: I watched a film last night.

options: We moved here three years ago.
We moved here ago three years.
We moved here three ago years.
questions.answer: We moved here three years ago.

options: She worked in a cafe last summer.
She workeds in a cafe last summer.
She works in a cafe last summer.
questions.answer: She worked in a cafe last summer.
questions.explanation: Past form is the same for all persons: worked.

topic: past simple: irregular verbs (go, have, get...)
rule_en: Many common verbs are irregular in the past: go → went, have → had, get → got, buy → bought, see → saw, come → came, take → took. Negatives and questions use did/didn't + base verb for ALL verbs.
structure: irregular past form; did/didn't + base verb
examples_en: We went to the mountains on New Year's Eve.
She had a big party for her birthday.
I got a lovely present from my sister.
Did you see the fireworks? — Yes, I did.
tip: After did/didn't always use the base form: 'Did you go?', not 'Did you went?'

options: We went to the beach yesterday.
We goed to the beach yesterday.
We did went to the beach yesterday.
questions.answer: We went to the beach yesterday.

questions.text: Choose the question: ___ you have a good time?
questions.explanation: Past questions: Did + subject + base verb.

questions.text: Choose the negative: I ___ my homework.

options: She took a lot of photos.
She taked a lot of photos.
She did took a lot of photos.
questions.answer: She took a lot of photos.

rule_en: In stories we mix regular and irregular past forms. Word order stays the same as in the present. Questions: Did + subject + base verb. Negatives: didn't + base verb. Short answers: Yes, I did / No, I didn't.
structure: past simple in positive, negative and question forms
examples_en: The detective opened the door and saw a dark room.
Nobody heard the shot.
Why did she leave the party early?
He didn't say a word all evening.
tip: Learn irregular verbs in groups with the same pattern: know–knew, grow–grew, throw–threw.

options: Why did he call the police?
Why did he called the police?
questions.answer: Why did he call the police?

questions.text: Choose the negative: They ___ anything strange.

options: She did knew the answer immediately.

questions.text: Choose the short answer: Did you lock the door? — No, I ___.

topic: there is / there are; some / any
rule_en: Use there is + singular and there are + plural to say what exists. In positive sentences use some with plurals (There are some chairs). In negatives and questions use any (There aren't any pictures. Are there any shelves?).
structure: There is/are (+ some); there isn't/aren't + any; Is/Are there any...?
examples_en: There's a big sofa in the living room.
There are some plants near the window.
There aren't any cupboards in this room.
Is there a balcony in your flat?
tip: some = positive, any = negative and questions.

questions.text: Choose the correct form: ___ two bedrooms in the flat.
Choose the correct word: There are ___ books on the shelf.
Choose the correct word: There aren't ___ windows in the bathroom.
Choose the question: ___ there a garage?

options: Are there any good cafes near here?
Is there any good cafes near here?
Are there some good cafes near here usually?
questions.answer: Are there any good cafes near here?

options: There's a lamp on the desk.
There are a lamp on the desk.
There have a lamp on the desk.
questions.answer: There's a lamp on the desk.

rule_en: Talk about what existed in the past with there was + singular and there were + plural. Negative: there wasn't / there weren't. Questions: Was there...? Were there...?
structure: There was/were; there wasn't/weren't; Was/Were there...?
examples_en: There was an old piano in the hall.
There were strange noises at night.
There wasn't any light in the corridor.
Were there any guests in room 333?
tip: Same rule as the present: singular → was, plural → were.

questions.text: Choose the correct form: ___ a big garden behind the house.
Choose the correct form: ___ many old photos in the box.
Choose the negative: ___ any hot water in the hotel.
Choose the question: ___ there a lift in the building?

options: There weren't any towels in the bathroom.
There wasn't any towels in the bathroom.
There weren't some towels in the bathroom.
questions.answer: There weren't any towels in the bathroom.

questions.text: Choose the short answer: Were there many people? — Yes, there ___.

rule_en: Countable nouns have a plural (an egg, two eggs). Uncountable nouns have no plural and no a/an (rice, milk, bread). Use some/any with plurals and uncountables: some rice, any apples.
structure: a/an + countable singular; some/any + plural or uncountable
examples_en: I had an egg and some bread for breakfast.
Is there any milk in the fridge?
We need some rice for this dish.
She doesn't eat meat.
tip: Say 'a piece of bread' or 'a glass of water' to count uncountable things.

questions.text: Choose the correct word: I'd like ___ orange, please.
questions.explanation: Countable singular starting with a vowel → an.

questions.text: Choose the correct word: There's ___ cheese in the fridge.
Choose the correct word: Do we have ___ tomatoes?

options: I don't drink a coffee usually ever.
Can I have a glass of water?
Can I have a water glass of?
Can I have glass a of water?
questions.answer: Can I have a glass of water?

topic: quantifiers: how much / how many, a lot of...
rule_en: Use How many + countable plural (How many eggs?) and How much + uncountable (How much sugar?). A lot of works with both. Use much/many mostly in negatives and questions, a little + uncountable, a few + countable.
structure: How many + plural; How much + uncountable; a lot of / a little / a few
examples_en: How much sugar do you take in your tea?
How many bottles of water do we need?
There's a lot of salt in this soup.
Add a little oil and a few onions.
tip: not much + uncountable, not many + plural: 'not much time', 'not many friends'.

questions.text: Choose the correct word: How ___ bread do we have?
Choose the correct word: How ___ eggs are in the box?
Choose the correct word: There's ___ milk left — buy some more.
Choose the correct word: I only need ___ potatoes.

options: We don't have a few time.
She drinks a lot of tea.
questions.answer: She drinks a lot of tea.

rule_en: Short adjectives add -er: cheap → cheaper, big → bigger, easy → easier. Long adjectives use more: more expensive. Irregular: good → better, bad → worse, far → further. Use than to compare: Tea is cheaper than coffee.
examples_en: This restaurant is cheaper than the one near the station.
The exam was more difficult than last year.
My new phone is better than my old one.
The traffic is worse in the evening.
tip: One-syllable: -er; three or more syllables: more; two syllables — check the dictionary.

options: This street is quieter than mine.
This street is more quiet than mine always.
This street is quieter that mine.
questions.answer: This street is quieter than mine.

rule_en: Superlatives compare one thing with all the others in a group. Short adjectives: the + -est (the oldest). Long adjectives: the most + adjective (the most dangerous). Irregular: the best, the worst, the furthest.
examples_en: It's the oldest building in the city.
This is the most dangerous road in the country.
Which is the best cafe near here?
That was the worst journey of my life.
tip: After superlatives we often use 'in': the tallest building in the world.

options: It's the highest mountain in Asia.
It's the highest mountain of Asia at all.
It's the most high mountain in Asia.
questions.answer: It's the highest mountain in Asia.

options: This is the most interesting museum in town.
This is most interesting museum in town.
This is the interestingest museum in town.
questions.answer: This is the most interesting museum in town.

topic: be going to (plans); future time expressions
rule_en: Use be going to + verb for plans and intentions: I'm going to visit five countries. Future time expressions: tomorrow, next week, next month, in two days, this summer.
structure: subject + be + going to + base verb
examples_en: We're going to travel around Europe next summer.
She's going to book the tickets tonight.
I'm not going to take a taxi — the metro is faster.
Are you going to see the Eiffel Tower?
tip: With the verb 'go' you can shorten: 'We're going to the beach' instead of 'going to go'.

questions.text: Choose the correct form: I ___ visit my aunt tomorrow.
Choose the correct form: They ___ to move to a new flat.
Choose the question: ___ she going to study abroad?
Choose the negative: We ___ going to stay long.

options: He's going to buy a car next month.
He's going to buys a car next month.
He's going buy a car next month.
questions.answer: He's going to buy a car next month.

rule_en: Use be going to also for predictions when we can see evidence now: Look at those clouds — it's going to rain. The structure is the same as for plans.
structure: subject + be + going to + base verb (prediction)
examples_en: Careful! You're going to drop the glasses.
It's very late — we're going to miss the train.
Look at the sky. It's going to snow.
She plays every day. She's going to be a great player.
tip: Prediction with evidence now → going to.

questions.text: Choose the correct form: Look at those clouds! It ___ rain.

options: Slow down! We're going to have an accident!
Slow down! We go to have an accident!
Slow down! We're going have an accident!
questions.answer: Slow down! We're going to have an accident!

questions.text: Choose the correct form: The team plays very well. They ___ win.
Choose the negative: Don't worry, you ___ fall.
Choose the question: ___ it going to be cold tomorrow?
questions.explanation: be + subject + going to in questions.

options: She's going to be famous one day.
She's go to be famous one day.
She going to is famous one day.
questions.answer: She's going to be famous one day.

rule_en: Adverbs of manner say how we do something. Most are adjective + -ly: slow → slowly, careful → carefully. Irregular: good → well, fast → fast, hard → hard. They usually go after the verb or object.
examples_en: Please speak slowly — I'm still learning.
She sings really well.
He works very hard.
They welcomed us warmly.
tip: 'Hardly' is NOT the adverb of 'hard' — it means 'almost not'.

questions.explanation: hard = with effort; hardly = almost not.

rule_en: Some verbs are followed by to + infinitive: want, need, decide, hope, plan, learn, try, forget, promise. Example: I want to see the world. She decided to buy the tickets.
examples_en: I want to learn to drive.
We decided to spend less money on things.
She hopes to visit Japan one day.
Don't forget to call me.
tip: After 'would like' also use to + infinitive: I'd like to try.

questions.text: Choose the correct form: I want ___ a new language.
Choose the correct form: They decided ___ at home.
Choose the correct form: She's learning ___ the piano.

options: We hope to see you soon.
questions.answer: We hope to see you soon.

questions.text: Choose the correct form: I need ___ some money.

topic: definite article: the or no the
rule_en: Use the when both speakers know which thing we mean, or when there is only one (the sun, the internet). Don't use the with general plurals and uncountables (I love music), with meals, most streets, languages and 'go home / go to work / go to bed'.
structure: the + specific noun; no article + general noun
examples_en: I found the article you sent me.
I read news on the internet every morning.
She loves music and plays the piano.
We had dinner and went home.
tip: Musical instruments take 'the': play the guitar; sports don't: play football.

options: We play the tennis on Saturdays.
We play a tennis on Saturdays.
I go to bed at eleven.

rule_en: Form the present perfect with have/has + past participle: I have seen, she has been. Use it for experiences at an unspecified time: I've seen this film ten times. Past participles: regular = -ed; irregular: see → seen, be → been, do → done, eat → eaten.
examples_en: I've seen this film three times.
She's been to twenty countries.
We've eaten at this restaurant before.
Have you ever done a bungee jump?
tip: 'Been' vs 'gone': He's been to Paris (and returned) / He's gone to Paris (he's still there).

rule_en: Use the present perfect for experiences without a specific time (I've been to Rome). Use the past simple when we say WHEN (I went to Rome in 2023). Time markers: ever/never/before → present perfect; yesterday, last year, ago, in 2020 → past simple.
structure: no time → present perfect; finished time → past simple
examples_en: I've never tried horse milk.
She visited Istanbul last spring.
Have you ever met a famous person? — Yes, I met an actor two years ago.
We've travelled a lot, but we didn't travel anywhere last year.
tip: If the answer says WHEN, switch to the past simple.

rule_en: Review of questions: with be invert the verb (Are you...?); with other verbs use do/does (present) or did (past); with can put it first (Can you...?); with the present perfect use have/has (Have you ever...?). Question word always comes first.
examples_en: Where were you born?
What do you do at weekends?
Did you study English at school?
How long have you lived here?
tip: Choose the auxiliary by tense: do/does → present, did → past, have/has → present perfect.

questions.explanation: 'Born' goes with 'be': Where were you born?
